cards.def: Honorius was the Roman emperor who recalled the troops from Britain. That left the Britons defenseless, as the video on Roman to Anglo-Saxon Britain explains.

The Angles, Saxons and Jutes were the Germanic tribes who came to Britain as mercenaries after the Romans left and then took the island over, the Jutes settling Kent, the Saxons Essex, Wessex and Sussex, and the Angles East Anglia, Mercia and Northumbria. They matter because their takeover began the Anglo-Saxon period and their Germanic speech became Old English, and the name Anglo-Saxon comes from the Angles and the Saxons.

Alfred the Great was the first true English king, and he united the kingdoms against the Danes. He created the fyrd, written law, a fleet, the Witan and the shires, and he commissioned the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle. He also supported Latin learning and Bede's Ecclesiastical History.
Bede was a monk who wrote the Ecclesiastical History of the English People. It is our main source for the period, and it contains Caedmon's Hymn.
Caedmon was an illiterate cowherd who became a poet. His Caedmon's Hymn is the earliest poem recorded in English.

The Vikings, also called the Danes, were raiders who attacked England and then settled permanently in eastern Britain, in the area called the Danelaw. They matter because, as the common enemy, they united the Anglo-Saxon kingdoms under Alfred the Great, and they gave English around 2,000 words such as 'give', 'take' and 'die'.
Edward the Confessor was the Anglo-Saxon king who built Westminster Abbey. He died childless, which triggered the fight over who would succeed him.
Harold Godwinson was the Earl of Wessex, and the Witan chose him as king after Edward the Confessor died. He lost the crown to William at the Battle of Hastings.

William the Conqueror, also called William I, was the Duke of Normandy who led the Norman Conquest and became king of England. He put a French-speaking ruling class in power, gave land to Norman vassals, built 5,000 to 6,000 castles and ordered the Domesday Survey. He also made all landholders swear loyalty to him.
Geoffrey of Monmouth wrote the History of the Kings of Britain in Latin. It is the source of the Arthurian legends.
Marie de France wrote the Lais in Anglo-Norman French. She drew them from Breton sources.
The Gawain poet, also called the Pearl poet, is the anonymous author of Sir Gawain and the Green Knight. The poem belongs to the Alliterative Revival and survives in only one manuscript.

Geoffrey Chaucer wrote The Canterbury Tales in Middle English, mostly in rhymed couplets with five-stress lines, and he also wrote Troilus and Criseyde. As the son of a wine merchant, he stands for the rising merchant class.
William Langland wrote Piers Plowman. It is an alliterative dream vision that criticizes society and the Church after the plague, and it describes the July 'hungry gap'.
John Wycliffe was a reformer who attacked corruption in the Church. His followers, the Lollards, began the first complete English Bible.

The Lollards were the followers of John Wycliffe who attacked corruption in the Church and produced the first complete English Bible. They matter because they challenged Church authority and put scripture into English, and they were persecuted and burned as heretics.
Julian of Norwich wrote the Book of Showings. It is a Christian visionary text, part of the important fourteenth-century trend of Christian visionary writing.
Margery Kempe is the author of The Book of Margery Kempe, an account of her own life and religious experiences.
Sir Thomas Malory wrote Le Morte Darthur while in prison. It is the great prose collection of Arthurian romance, and William Caxton printed it.
William Caxton set up England's first printing press. His moveable type made fast, identical copies possible, and he printed Malory's Morte Darthur.
Henry VII, also called Henry Tudor, won the Battle of Bosworth Field and married Elizabeth of York, ending the Wars of the Roses. He began the Tudor dynasty, which is where the Middle Ages end.
Henry VIII dissolved the monasteries. That ended their role as England's main producers of books.
